title: HoldExpiredException replaces the ConflictException and no handler maps it: a 500 instead of a 409
summary: The developer gives the expired-hold case of `POST /orders` its own exception, `HoldExpiredException`, carrying the hold id, so that callers and logs can tell it from the other conflicts, and leaves `ApiErrors`, the `@RestControllerAdvice`, as it was. The new class extends `RuntimeException`, not `ConflictException`, so no `@ExceptionHandler` takes it and no `@ResponseStatus` marks it: a client that places an order for an expired hold now gets a 500 from the container's error page instead of the 409 problem detail. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now lists under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under `POST /orders`: `throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500`.

change.description: Add `HoldExpiredException`, a `RuntimeException` that carries the hold id, and throw it from `OrderService.place` where `ConflictException("hold ... has expired")` was thrown. `ApiErrors` is not touched: its handlers are for `NotFoundException`, `ConflictException` and `InvalidRequestException`.

risk: Spring resolves an exception at request time: `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver` looks for an `@ExceptionHandler` in the controller and then in the advices whose parameter type the exception extends, `ResponseStatusExceptionResolver` for a `@ResponseStatus` on the exception's class, and `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver` for the framework's own exceptions. `HoldExpiredException` extends `RuntimeException` and nothing else, so none of them applies, the servlet container's error page answers, and `POST /orders` for a hold that expired returns a 500 with no problem detail, where the API contract (and the system test, which needs Docker and Kafka) says 409. A client that retries on 5xx, as clients do, retries a request that will fail the same way until the hold is held again. Nothing before deployment notices: the exception compiles, the context starts (handlers are matched per exception, not registered against a list), and the unit tests of `OrderService` assert the exception type, which is what the developer changed them to. A reviewer sees a new exception class and a one-line change of what is thrown, both of which read as the refactoring they are.
explanation: The boundary contract lists under each route what it throws, found by following the calls from the handler through the module's own classes (`OrderController.place` to `OrderService.place` to the lambda it hands `Transactions.run`), with what each exception becomes: `ConflictException (409 by ApiErrors.conflict)`, `NotFoundException (404 by ApiErrors.notFound)`, `IllegalStateException (500)`. The developer sees a refactoring, so the runner regenerates the contract and the reviewer reads the diff: under `POST /orders` the throws line gains `HoldExpiredException (500)` and loses nothing a reviewer would expect it to lose (the other conflicts of the route still throw `ConflictException`), and a new line follows it, `! throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500`. The `!` line is the violation. `IllegalStateException (500)` on the same route is not one: it is the JDK's exception from a guard that fired (`Transactions.requireActive`, a concurrent status change), a 500 by design, and the contract lists it without a `!`.
resolution: Make `HoldExpiredException` extend `ConflictException`, so `ApiErrors.conflict` takes it and the line reads `HoldExpiredException (409 by ApiErrors.conflict)`; or add an `@ExceptionHandler` for it to `ApiErrors`, with the status and the problem detail the case deserves (a 409 with the hold id, or a 410); or put `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)` on the class, which answers the status but not the problem body the other errors have. Each removes the `!` line; the diff the reviewer approves then shows the new exception under the route with its status, which is the change the developer meant.
notes: The first example of the throws lines and the exception outcomes of a boundary contract (`lib/src/failures.rs` for the outcomes, `Graph::throws` in `lib/src/reach.rs` for the exceptions). The exceptions come from the same call graph as the reach lines: a `throw` of a `new`, of a typed local, of what a method returned or a cast produced, the supplier of an `Optional.orElseThrow` (the lambda's return type, or `NoSuchElementException` with no supplier), and Spring's `Assert` (`IllegalStateException` for `state`, `IllegalArgumentException` for the rest). A `catch` on the path that never rethrows its variable swallows what it catches (`HoldService.hold` turns `HoldPolicy`'s `IllegalArgumentException` into `InvalidRequestException` this way); one that does rethrow it, like the retry loop in `Transactions.run` or a `finally`, passes everything through; one that wraps throws the wrapper. An `@Async` callee of another class throws on its own thread. The compiler's own guards, the `MatchException` of an exhaustive switch over a sealed type and an `assert`, are left out.

What each exception becomes follows Spring's resolution order: an `@ExceptionHandler` in the controller (or a superclass of it) first, then the `@ControllerAdvice` beans in `@Order` (ties by class name), each matched by its `basePackages`, `assignableTypes` and `annotations` when it names any, the closest type up the exception's superclass chain winning within one bean; then a `@ResponseStatus` on the exception's class or a superclass; then the status a `ResponseStatusException` was built with, when it is an `HttpStatus` constant. A handler's status is its `@ResponseStatus`, else the first `HttpStatus` constant its body loads (`ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, ...)`), else the literal it passes to `ResponseEntity.status`, else the handler is named without a status. Two `@ExceptionHandler` methods for one type in one advice are a `!` line: Spring refuses the ambiguity when it builds the advice's resolver at startup.

Only an exception type of the module's own (or a sibling module's) that nothing maps is a `!` line. A JDK or framework exception that reaches a route is listed as `(500)` without one: `IllegalStateException` from `Transactions.requireActive` or from a concurrent status change in `OrderTransitions`, `IllegalArgumentException` from `HoldPolicy.totalCents`, are guards, and a 500 is what a guard that fired should be. The regenerated Box Office contracts list these under the routes of the ticketing service (the hold route throws five kinds), with no `!` line: every application exception of the three modules has its handler. What the lines do not see: an exception a framework or driver call throws (`DataAccessException`, `OptimisticLockingFailureException`, a Kafka timeout), a `throws` clause, an exception built in a way the walk cannot type, a handler status computed at run time, and a `ControllerAdvice` ordered by `Ordered` or `@Priority` rather than `@Order`. A `@KafkaListener` or `@Scheduled` method gets its `throws` line without outcomes: the container's error handler (retries, a dead-letter topic, a log line) decides, and that configuration is not read.

The runner compiles the module with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`; the module's Spring Boot tests need Docker for Testcontainers, and are recorded as the tests' result. By hand, `./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun` with the patch applied reports the `POST /orders` route changed, its throws line now ending in `HoldExpiredException (500)` with the `!` line under it, and `1 problems` in the module's statistics.
provenance: Constructed from the way Spring MVC resolves exceptions (`HandlerExceptionResolverComposite`: handler methods, then `@ResponseStatus`, then the framework's own, else the container's error page) and from a refactoring every service makes at some point, giving a case its own exception type so that callers can tell it apart; the expired hold of `POST /orders` is the Box Office case most likely to get one, since it is the only conflict the client can resolve by itself, by holding the seats again.
